message.content:
**Short‑answer:**  
Painting the entire Eiffel Tower would normally take **about two to three years** when you work continuously under ideal conditions—assuming a dedicated crew, modern spray‑painting rigs, and no major interruptions from weather or logistics.

---

### Why it’s so long

| Factor | How it adds time |
|--------|------------------|
| **Surface area** | Roughly 12–15 k m² of exposed steel (including rails, girders, and decorative elements) – far larger than most skyscrapers because of its lattice design. |
| **Access & safety** | Workers cannot simply climb up like they do on ordinary buildings. Rope‑access teams, climbing harnesses, temporary platforms, and sometimes even helicopters are used. Every move needs careful planning and inspection. |
| **Preparation** | Old paint must be removed mechanically or chemically, rust patches treated, and primers applied before the protective topcoat. That prep alone can consume several months. |
| **Coating process** | Modern high‑performance paints require at least **three coats** (primer + two finishes). After each coat there’s a mandatory cure period (often 24–48 h) plus quality checks. |
| **Weather constraints** | Wind speeds above 20 km/h, rain, snow, or extreme temperatures halt spraying operations entirely. In Paris this means roughly 60–70% usable working days per year. |
| **Logistics** | Delivering thousands of liters of paint, setting up cranes, securing permits, coordinating with city traffic—all add overhead. |

---

### A ball‑park math walk‑through

Assume:

* One skilled painter can cover ≈ 30 m²/day (typical for industrial spray systems).
* You have a team of **50 painters** operating simultaneously (the real crew often ranges between 40–80 people depending on budget).

\[
\text{Daily coverage} = 50 \times 30\,\mathrm{m^2}=1500\,\mathrm{m^2}
\]

If we target **13 k m²** of new coating (after prep):

\[
\frac{13000}{1500}\;\text{days}\approx8.7\;\text{calendar days}
\]

But remember:

* Only **≈ 200 working days/year** are available after accounting for weather, holidays, inspections, and downtime.
* Three coats → × 3 ⇒ ≈ 26 calendar days *per season*, but spread across seasons.
* Prep and curing stages double the effective “paint” time.

So, while raw productivity suggests < one month, practical realities push the overall effort into the **two‑year range**.

---

### Real‑world precedent

When the French government undertook a comprehensive repaint of the Eiffel Tower in 2019–2020, the project was scheduled for **six months**, but only covered selected sections (e.g., the uppermost tier). Full‑tower repaints happen infrequently—typically once every decade or longer—to preserve structural integrity without excessive disruption.

---

#### Bottom line

A complete overhaul of the Eiffel Tower’s exterior paint job isn’t a quick weekend gig—it’s a multi‑phase engineering operation that usually spans **roughly 2–3 years** when executed back‑to‑back. If you’re looking at just a single section or touch‑up, expect a few weeks to a couple of months, depending on scope and site restrictions.
